problem_motivation.content: Bandgap-limited absorption and thermalization degrade TPV/PV performance
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, the photon absorption of a solar cell is constrained by the bandgap of its semiconductor material [4]. Additionally, the absorption of photons with energies well above the bandgap degrades PV cell performance due to thermalization.

problem_motivation.content: Designing a narrowband emitter requires simultaneously balancing multiple competing spectral objectives
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, the most challenging task in achieving a narrowband response is to simultaneously optimize several competing parameters: a strong emission peak, a wavelength of peak emission to be inside the absorption range of the PV cell, a minimal FWHM with an emission range slightly above the PV cell’s absorption cut-off, and very low out-of-band emission.

problem_motivation.content: Only a limited part of parameter space yields promising narrowband designs, motivating efficient optimization
problem_motivation.evidence_span: this dataset visualization indicates that the design landscape features both structured, high-performance areas and numerous underperforming regions, highlighting the need for an efficient optimization strategy to systematically identify promising emitter geometries.

problem_motivation.content: Promising candidates occupy only a small region of parameter space, so efficient optimization is needed
problem_motivation.evidence_span: these statistics indicate that the dataset contains promising narrowband candidates, but they occupy only a limited portion of the overall parameter space, suggesting that an efficient optimization method is required to effectively find the optimized design parameters for the required performance.

problem_motivation.content: Emitter optical properties change with temperature, so temperature-dependent ITO optics must be evaluated before electrothermal analysis
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The TPV cell’s electrical performance strongly depends on the emitter’s emission spectrum, which changes with temperature because the emitter material’s optical characteristics are temperature-dependent. For this reason, before proceeding with the electrothermal analysis, the complex refractive index of the ITO material at different temperatures was evaluated

problem_motivation.content: No single prior study provided both broad-wavelength optical constants and suitable operating-temperature dependence for ITO
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Since no single published work provided both the necessary broad-wavelength optical constants and an appropriate analysis of their operating-temperature dependence

prior_approach.content: Prior solutions included back-surface reflectors, altered geometries, and multijunction cells
prior_approach.evidence_span: Previous research recommended numerous solutions to address this issue. Few studies have focused on incorporating a back-surface reflector, altering cell geometry, or developing a multi-junction cell rather than a single-junction cell [5–13].

prior_approach.content: Photonic-crystal selective emitters are an established route for selective emission
prior_approach.evidence_span: In contrast to homogeneous materials, photonic crystal-based selective emitters are found to be a powerful route to achieving selective emission since these multilayer-periodic structures can support different types of resonance modes like Fabry–Pérot (FP) cavity and guided mode resonance and can support epsilon-near-zero effects [18–20].

prior_approach.content: Prior photonic-crystal emitters used refractory materials such as Mo, Ta, W, Pt, Si, and Ir with dielectrics
prior_approach.evidence_span: Till now, various high-temperature stable refractory materials, such as molybdenum (Mo), tantalum (Ta), tungsten (W), platinum (Pt), silicon (Si), and iridium (Ir), based structures with various dielectric materials, have been used in photonic crystal-based emitters [21, 22].

prior_approach.content: Recent all-oxide emitters based on CeO2/MgO and YSZ/MgO were proposed
prior_approach.evidence_span: Recently, Song et al proposed all-oxide emitters based on CeO2/MgO and YSZ/MgO composite multilayer structures [25].

prior_approach.content: A common design strategy is forward modeling with parameter sweeps
prior_approach.evidence_span: A general strategy for designing such photonic structures is forward modeling, in which the geometric parameters of a specified structure are tuned until the desired spectral response is achieved.

prior_approach.content: ITO-Al2O3 architectures were previously demonstrated experimentally for wavelength-selective thermal emission
prior_approach.evidence_span: Indeed, ITO–Al2O3 architectures have previously been experimentally demonstrated for wavelength-selective thermal emission [28].

prior_approach.content: Prior high-temperature studies examined ITO thin-film stability and functionality
prior_approach.evidence_span: Furthermore, high-temperature studies have demonstrated that ITO thin films can retain useful optical and electrical functionality at elevated temperatures, although their properties depend on crystallinity, oxygen partial pressure, deposition conditions, and the underlying substrate [29–31].

prior_approach.content: Gregory et al. reported ITO films on alumina stayed stable after 1400 °C exposure
prior_approach.evidence_span: Gregory et al. reported that ITO films deposited on alumina remained structurally and chemically stable even after exposure to 1400 ◦C (1673 K)

prior_approach.content: Kim et al. found temperature-induced ITO optical-property changes are systematic and reversible under controlled oxygen pressure
prior_approach.evidence_span: More recently, Kim et al. demonstrated that although the optical properties of ITO evolve with temperature because of electron–phonon interactions and oxygen-vacancy redistribution, these changes are systematic and reversible under controlled oxygen partial pressure, indicating that ITO retains its functional optical characteristics at elevated temperatures [30].

prior_approach.content: Li et al. reported stable conductivity and microstructure of ITO during prolonged 1000 °C operation
prior_approach.evidence_span: In addition, Li et al. reported stable electrical conductivity and microstructural stability of ITO films during prolonged operation at 1000 ◦C, confirming their suitability for harsh thermal environments [31].

prior_approach.content: Del Villar et al. provided room-temperature n and k data used as the 300 K reference
prior_approach.evidence_span: the room-temperature refractive index (𝑛) and extinction coefficient (𝑘) data reported by Del Villar et al. at 300 K

prior_approach.content: D'Elia et al. provided Drude-Lorentz analysis used to interpret model parameters
prior_approach.evidence_span: The Drude-Lorentz analysis presented by D’Elia et al. was utilized to substantiate the physical interpretation of the model parameters

prior_approach.content: Silva-Oelker et al. studied W/HfO2/W and Mo/HfO2/Mo emitters with GaSb cells
prior_approach.evidence_span: Silva-Oelker et al. investigated W/HfO2/W and Mo/HfO2/Mo disk-array emitters coupled to GaSb cells in the far field.

prior_approach.content: Zhao et al. reported a W/Al2O3 Fabry-Perot emitter with a GaInAsSb cell
prior_approach.evidence_span: The W/Al2O3 multilayer Fabry–Pérot emitter reported by Zhao et al. was coupled to a GaInAsSb cell

prior_approach.content: Li et al. reported a Ta/SiO2 cross-patch emitter with InGaAsSb and tandem cells
prior_approach.evidence_span: Li et al. reported a Ta/SiO2 cross-patch metamaterial emitter with a narrow emission peak near 1.70 𝜇m and when the emitter was coupled to InGaAsSb and Si/InGaAsSb tandem photovoltaic configurations

prior_approach.content: Rong et al. studied an emitter-only Ge/SiO2/Au nanocylinder design
prior_approach.evidence_span: Rong et al., focused on an emitter-only Ge/SiO2/Au nanocylinder configuration exhibiting an extremely narrow spectral response and high directionality

prior_approach.content: Hasuike et al. demonstrated an ITO diffraction grating using thermal nanoimprint lithography and RF sputtering
prior_approach.evidence_span: Hasuike et al. used thermal nanoimprint lithography in conjunction with RF sputtering to experimentally demonstrate an ITO diffraction-grating structure [41]

prior_approach.content: Dao et al. demonstrated scalable colloidal lithography for patterned ITO selective emitters
prior_approach.evidence_span: Dao et al. demonstrated scalable colloidal lithography for patterned ITO-based selective thermal emitters [28].

prior_approach.content: Al2O3 thin films have been anisotropically dry etched using BCl3/Cl2/Ar plasmas
prior_approach.evidence_span: Anisotropic dry etching of Al2O3 thin films has been experimentally demonstrated using such plasma chemistries [43].

prior_approach.content: Yoon et al. demonstrated controlled dry etching of ITO-containing multilayers with H2/HCl high-density plasma
prior_approach.evidence_span: Yoon et al. provided an experimental foundation for anisotropic pattern transfer in ITO by demonstrating controlled dry etching of ITO-containing multilayer structures using H2/HCl-based high-density plasma [44].

prior_approach.content: FDTD-generated dataset spectra were used to train ExtraTrees surrogate models.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The narrowband emission FOMs of the dataset spectra obtained from FDTD analysis were subsequently used to train ExtraTrees surrogate models.

prior_limitation.content: These prior TPV/PV approaches have manufacturability, cost, and recombination drawbacks
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Despite their performance potential, back-surface reflectors can suffer from parasitic absorption in reflector stacks and elevated surface recombination, requiring stringent passivation, while multijunction solar cells remain limited by complex fabrication, extremely high manufacturing costs, and series-connected current-matching sensitivity to spectral variations; on the other hand, complex geometries often increase surface-area-driven recombination and impose difficult passivation and fabrication requirements, which negatively impact practical manufacturability [14–17].

prior_limitation.content: Refractory-material emitters suffer oxidation at high temperature
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Although refractory materials exhibit high thermal stability, they are prone to oxidation at high temperatures, which can severely degrade the structure’s optical performance and thermal stability [23].

prior_limitation.content: Song et al.'s all-oxide emitter was not narrowband and had low peak amplitude
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, their designed emitter exhibited a non-narrowband emission spectrum with low peak amplitude.

prior_limitation.content: High-fidelity parameter sweeps are inefficient and computationally expensive
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, such a parameter-sweep approach for high-fidelity predictions is inefficient and computationally expensive due to the large number of degrees of freedom.

prior_limitation.content: Directly choosing from the discrete sampled candidates cannot refine geometry continuously because of nonlinearity and trade-offs
prior_limitation.evidence_span: the pronounced nonlinearity and trade-offs observed across the design space make direct selection from the sampled candidates insufficient for continuous geometric refinement.

prior_limitation.content: Those higher reported efficiencies were under different PV architectures and operating conditions
prior_limitation.evidence_span: These higher efficiencies, however, correspond to different photovoltaic architectures and operating conditions from those considered in the present work.

prior_limitation.content: Rong et al. did not analyze photovoltaic conversion, so only optical comparison is appropriate
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Since that study did not include photovoltaic conversion analysis, its performance is more appropriately compared in terms of spectral selectivity and angular behavior rather than electrical efficiency.

rejected_alternative.content: Instead of using wide-bandgap oxides as the main absorber, the design uses ITO as the absorptive medium because Al2O3 mainly provides confinement and matching
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: In contrast, wide-bandgap dielectric oxides such as Al2O3 generally exhibit comparatively low optical loss in the near-infrared and therefore primarily provide dielectric confinement, phase control, and impedance matching rather than acting as the principal absorptive medium.

rejected_alternative.content: Rather than aiming for highest efficiency alone, the work emphasizes an all-oxide oxidation-resistant platform integrated with inverse design, verification, thermal optics, angular analysis, and electrothermal simulation
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Although the proposed configuration does not provide the highest conversion efficiency among the systems listed in Table 1, its distinguishing feature is the integration of an all-oxide, oxidation-resistant emitter architecture with surrogate-assisted Bayesian inverse design, direct FDTD verification, temperature-dependent ITO optical modeling, angular-response analysis, and cell-level electrothermal simulation within a unified computational framework.

causal_claim.content: Challenges of forward modeling motivate inverse design
causal_claim.evidence_span: These challenges lead to the inverse-design method, in which the design task is framed as an optimization problem: given a specified spectral requirement, identify the structural parameters that most effectively satisfy it.

causal_claim.content: Machine learning and surrogate modeling have accelerated inverse design by replacing repeated simulations
causal_claim.evidence_span: Recent progress in machine learning (ML) and surrogate modeling has expedited inverse design by substituting costly repeated simulations with data-driven models that estimate the relationship between design parameters and performance metrics.

causal_claim.content: A trained surrogate enables much faster assessment and exploration than full-wave simulation
causal_claim.evidence_span: After being trained on a sufficiently extensive simulation database, a surrogate model can assess potential designs significantly more quickly than full-wave simulation, enabling effective exploration of continuous parameter spaces.

causal_claim.content: Bayesian optimization improves the process by balancing exploitation and exploration probabilistically
causal_claim.evidence_span: Bayesian optimization improves this process by probabilistically selecting new candidate designs, effectively balancing the exploitation of promising areas with the exploration of uncertain ones.

causal_claim.content: Removing the metal phase by using only oxides can improve thermal stability
causal_claim.evidence_span: Using only oxide-based structures, the metal phase of the composite emitter structure can be eradicated.

causal_claim.content: Alumina forms an ITO-Al2O3 solid solution at high temperature, stabilizing ITO and preserving integrity
causal_claim.evidence_span: Alumina forms an ITO-Al2O3 solid solution at high temperatures, thereby stabilizing the ITO layer and maintaining its structural integrity.

causal_claim.content: SRH recombination significantly limits TPV-cell efficiency
causal_claim.evidence_span: The Shockley–Read–Hall (SRH) mechanism is the major non-radiative recombination process, which significantly limits the efficiency of TPV cell.

causal_claim.content: Recombination reduces excess carriers and directly affects electrical performance
causal_claim.evidence_span: the recombination term reduces the excess carrier population and directly affects the cell’s electrical performance parameters.

causal_claim.content: Higher operating temperature increases intrinsic carrier concentration and recombination, boosting dark current and reducing performance metrics
causal_claim.evidence_span: In general, at elevated temperatures, the material’s intrinsic carrier concentration and recombination rate increase, which enhances the dark current and mainly reduces 𝑉oc, fill factor, maximum output power, and efficiency.

causal_claim.content: Peak emission varies strongly with Al2O3 and ITO thicknesses, as set by period P
causal_claim.evidence_span: the large peak emission is highly non-uniform along the design space and depends strongly on specific values of 𝑡Al2O3 and 𝑡ITO, which is determined by 𝑃.

causal_claim.content: Period strongly affects whether strong resonant emission is enhanced or suppressed
causal_claim.evidence_span: the first one is that the period plays an important role in facilitating or minimizing strong resonant emission

causal_claim.content: Layer-thickness interference and coupling shift the resonant emission
causal_claim.evidence_span: the diagonal-banded patterns indicate a shift in resonant emission due to interference and coupling conditions arising from layer thicknesses in multilayer periodic structures.

causal_claim.content: High peak emissivity alone does not determine narrowband quality
causal_claim.evidence_span: a high peak emissivity does not uniquely determine narrowband quality: many designs achieve similar 𝐸peak while exhibiting substantially larger FWHM and 𝑅side levels.

causal_claim.content: Larger RMSE than MAE indicates some samples have large prediction errors
causal_claim.evidence_span: when RMSE is noticeably larger than MAE, it indicates the presence of a limited number of samples with relatively large prediction errors.

causal_claim.content: R2 close to 1 indicates strong predictive agreement, while lower R2 means incomplete reproduction of variation
causal_claim.evidence_span: A value close to unity indicates strong predictive agreement, whereas a lower value indicates that the surrogate does not fully reproduce the variation of that metric across the design space.

causal_claim.content: Closer parity-plot points to the diagonal mean more accurate predictions
causal_claim.evidence_span: data points closer to the diagonal line indicate more accurate surrogate predictions.

causal_claim.content: High R2 for peak emissivity means the surrogate captures most variation caused by geometric variables
causal_claim.evidence_span: The high 𝑅2 value indicates that the surrogate model captures most of the variation in peak emissivity produced by changes in the geometric design variables (𝑃, 𝑡ITO, 𝑡Al2O3).

causal_claim.content: FWHM prediction errors are larger for broad or multimode spectra because linewidth depends on spectral shape and half-maximum crossings
causal_claim.evidence_span: larger linewidth values, as expected, because FWHM depends on the detailed shape of the emissivity spectrum and on the accurate determination of the half-maximum crossing points. Spectra with shoulders, multiple peaks, or broad tails can therefore lead to larger linewidth-prediction errors.

causal_claim.content: Larger ΔR2 upon permutation means stronger dependence on that input parameter
causal_claim.evidence_span: a larger Δ𝑅2 indicates that disrupting the information contained in that parameter causes a greater deterioration in predictive performance and therefore signifies a stronger contribution to the corresponding spectral response.

causal_claim.content: Bandwidth and emission concentration are controlled jointly by resonant geometry and the ITO layer
causal_claim.evidence_span: the spectral bandwidth and concentration of emission are governed by the combined influence of the resonant geometry and the ITO layer.

causal_claim.content: Resonance position alone does not determine spectral selectivity
causal_claim.evidence_span: candidates with similar peak wavelengths can exhibit substantially different linewidths, demonstrating that resonance position alone does not determine the spectral selectivity of the emitter.

causal_claim.content: Designs with similar peak emissivity can still differ greatly in spectral concentration
causal_claim.evidence_span: designs with similar 𝐸peak may differ markedly in spectral concentration

causal_claim.content: Higher in-band fraction corresponds to cleaner narrowband behavior with less background spread
causal_claim.evidence_span: higher 𝑓in corresponds to cleaner narrowband behavior with reduced spectral spread into the background.

causal_claim.content: Localized electric field in lossy ITO promotes resonant optical dissipation
causal_claim.evidence_span: Since ITO exhibits appreciable optical loss in this spectral region, the localized electric field enhances the interaction between the resonant electromagnetic mode and the ITO layer, thereby promoting optical dissipation at the resonance wavelength.

causal_claim.content: With increasing temperature, Re(epsilon) becomes less negative in the IR because stronger Drude damping weakens the negative free-carrier contribution
causal_claim.evidence_span: With increasing temperature, Re(𝜀) becomes slightly less negative in the infrared region because the temperature-induced increase in the Drude damping reduces the magnitude of the negative free-carrier contribution.

causal_claim.content: Im(epsilon) increases with wavelength and temperature because free-carrier scattering and dissipation increase
causal_claim.evidence_span: This trend is attributed to enhanced free-carrier scattering and the resulting increase in optical dissipation at elevated temperatures.

causal_claim.content: Infrared refractive index increases more with temperature where Drude free-carrier response dominates
causal_claim.evidence_span: The temperature-induced increase in 𝑛 becomes more pronounced in the infrared region, where the Drude free-carrier response dominates the optical behavior of ITO.

causal_claim.content: Increasing temperature makes the resonance more damped and less spectrally confined, broadening linewidth and raising background emission
causal_claim.evidence_span: Consequently, the resonance becomes more strongly damped and less spectrally confined, leading to the progressive linewidth broadening and enhanced background emission observed in Fig. 10.

causal_claim.content: Placing the emission peak near the TPV bandgap is advantageous because above-bandgap photons generate carriers with less excess energy and lower thermalization loss
causal_claim.evidence_span: Such spectral positioning is advantageous for TPV conversion because photons emitted immediately above the semiconductor bandgap can contribute to photocarrier generation while carrying relatively little excess energy, thereby limiting thermalization losses associated with higher-energy photons.

causal_claim.content: At 1200 K, temperature-dependent ITO optics broaden and redshift the emission band
causal_claim.evidence_span: At a higher emitter operating temperature of 𝑇emi = 1200 K, the temperature-dependent optical response of ITO causes the principal emission band to broaden and shift toward longer wavelengths.

causal_claim.content: Spectral broadening can raise cell temperature by increasing carrier thermalization at shorter wavelengths
causal_claim.evidence_span: The spectral broadening can increase the cell temperature by enhancing carrier thermalization at shorter wavelengths.

causal_claim.content: Higher radiative loading causes substantial TPV self-heating
causal_claim.evidence_span: The increasing radiative loading consequently produces substantial self-heating of the photovoltaic device.

causal_claim.content: The benefit of stronger photogeneration is increasingly offset by temperature-induced recombination as the cell heats
causal_claim.evidence_span: the beneficial effect of increased photogeneration is progressively counteracted by temperature-induced recombination as the cell warms.

causal_claim.content: Above about 1200 K, rising Jsc cannot offset falling Voc and FF plus higher thermal loading, so efficiency drops
causal_claim.evidence_span: Beyond this operating point, the continued increase in 𝐽sc is insufficient to compensate for the simultaneous reductions in 𝑉oc and FF and the increasing thermal loading of the cell.

causal_claim.content: Jsc rises strongly with emitter temperature because thermal photon flux from the selective emitter increases rapidly
causal_claim.evidence_span: This behavior originates from the rapid increase in thermal photon flux emitted by the selective emitter at elevated temperatures.

causal_claim.content: Higher above-bandgap absorption increases photocarrier generation and Jsc
causal_claim.evidence_span: The resulting increase in above-bandgap photon absorption enhances the photocarrier-generation rate within the In0.73Ga0.27As cell and consequently increases 𝐽sc.

causal_claim.content: At high emitter temperatures, higher cell temperature raises intrinsic carrier concentration, strengthens recombination, and lowers Voc
causal_claim.evidence_span: the corresponding rise in cell temperature enhances the intrinsic carrier concentration, which intensifies carrier recombination and consequently reduces the achievable quasi-Fermi-level separation. As a result, 𝑉oc begins to decrease

causal_claim.content: Higher emitter temperature increases maximum power density mainly through higher Jsc
causal_claim.evidence_span: Increasing 𝑇emi substantially enhances the maximum obtainable power density because of the strong increase in 𝐽sc.

causal_claim.content: Voc decreases beyond about 1200 K, which reduces efficiency despite higher Jsc
causal_claim.evidence_span: the 𝑉oc decreases beyond temperature around 𝑇emi ≈1200 K, which leads to a decrease in efficiency beyond that temperature ... despite an increase 𝐽sc.

causal_claim.content: Lower cell temperature from active cooling mitigates recombination losses and preserves larger quasi-Fermi-level separation, improving Voc and J-V shape
causal_claim.evidence_span: The substantial reduction in cell temperature mitigates temperature-induced carrier-recombination losses and helps preserve a larger quasi-Fermi-level separation, thereby improving the open-circuit voltage and the overall shape of the 𝐽–𝑉 characteristic.

causal_claim.content: The squarer cooled J-V curve indicates improved fill factor
causal_claim.evidence_span: The increased squareness of the actively cooled 𝐽–𝑉 curve further indicates an improvement in the fill factor.

causal_claim.content: Power-output improvement comes mainly from recovered Voc and FF, not increased current
causal_claim.evidence_span: the enhancement in electrical output primarily originates from the recovery of 𝑉oc and the fill factor rather than from an increase in photogenerated current.

causal_claim.content: Active thermal management suppresses temperature-induced electrical losses and enables greater power extraction
causal_claim.evidence_span: reducing 𝑇cell from approximately 413 K to 310 K through active thermal management substantially suppresses temperature-induced electrical losses and enables greater power extraction from the TPV cell

causal_claim.content: Rising temperature increases free-carrier damping and broadens the emission peak.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The temperature-dependent optical performance analysis demonstrated that increasing temperature escalates free-carrier damping, leading to progressive broadening of the peak emission band.

causal_claim.content: Higher emitter temperature increases photogeneration and eventually cell temperature, which raises dark current and recombination losses.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The electrothermal analysis exhibited that increasing emitter temperature enhances photogeneration, and eventually the cell temperature, which progressively increases dark current losses and recombination.

causal_claim.content: Efficiency rises with emitter temperature and peaks near 1200 K with heat sinking.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Conse-quently, the conversion efficiency increased with emitter temperature and reached a maximum of approximately 32.17% near 𝑇emi = 1200 K with the heat sink configura-tion considered in this work.

mechanism_principle.content: Reducing oxygen diffusion at elevated temperature improves emitter thermal stability
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Thermal stability of the emitter can be improved by minimizing oxygen diffusion through it at elevated temperatures [24].

mechanism_principle.content: Alumina protects and stabilizes the structure while enabling ENZ-assisted resonances
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The alumina top layer serves as a chemically inert and thermally stable protective coating owing to its high melting point, excellent oxidation resistance, and negligible optical loss in the near-infrared, while simultaneously facilitating the excitation of ENZ-assisted optical resonances.

mechanism_principle.content: ITO was chosen because its free-carrier plasma response gives strong infrared dispersion and an ENZ transition
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The ITO layer was selected as the active emitting medium because its free-carrier plasma response produces a strongly dispersive optical response in the infrared, including an epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) transition between dielectric-like and metal-like regimes [26].

mechanism_principle.content: Near ENZ, small real permittivity enhances light-matter interaction, field localization, and absorption
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Near the ENZ condition, the small real part of the permittivity can enhance light–matter interaction and promote strong field localization and absorption when ITO is incorporated into an appropriately designed photonic structure [27].

mechanism_principle.content: Combining lossy dispersive ITO with low-loss Al2O3 enables spectrally selective resonant emission
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The combination of a dispersive, lossy ITO layer with a low-loss Al2O3 dielectric therefore provides a suitable platform for engineering spectrally selective resonant emission.

mechanism_principle.content: Gregory et al. attributed the stability to an interfacial ITO-Al2O3 region suppressing degradation
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: attributing this remarkable stability to the formation of an ITO–Al2O3 interfacial region that suppresses degradation beyond the temperature predicted by bulk thermodynamics [29].

mechanism_principle.content: ITO optical changes with temperature arise from electron-phonon interactions and oxygen-vacancy redistribution
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: the optical properties of ITO evolve with temperature because of electron–phonon interactions and oxygen-vacancy redistribution

mechanism_principle.content: Sapphire was selected for thermal stability, high melting point, strength, low NIR absorption, and oxide-film compatibility
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Finally, sapphire was selected as the substrate because of its exceptional thermal stability, high melting temperature, excellent mechanical strength, low optical absorption in the near-infrared, and excellent compatibility with oxide thin-film deposition.

mechanism_principle.content: ExtraTrees were used because they handle nonlinear data effectively
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Here, Extremely Randomized Trees (Extra-Trees) regressors were employed due to their effectiveness in handling nonlinear data.

mechanism_principle.content: Peak-wavelength prediction is difficult because mode switching can make lambda_peak jump abruptly between resonances
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This behavior arises because 𝜆peak can change abruptly when the dominant resonance switches from one spectral branch to another. In such cases, two resonant modes may have comparable emissivity, and a small change in geometry can cause the extracted maximum-emissivity wavelength to jump to a different mode.

mechanism_principle.content: In-band-fraction prediction is weaker because it depends on integrated in-band and out-of-band spectral energy
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This is because 𝑓in is an integrated spectral metric and depends on both the energy contained within the selected wavelength band and the total spectral emission outside that band. Consequently, small deviations in the predicted spectral distribution can influence the extracted value of 𝑓in.

mechanism_principle.content: ITO thickness controls peak emittance because it changes resonant-field interaction with lossy ITO and thus resonance strength and absorption
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: changing the ITO thickness modifies the interaction between the resonant electromagnetic field and the optically lossy ITO layer, thereby strongly affecting the resonance strength and associated absorption.

mechanism_principle.content: Period controls resonance wavelength by setting optical phase conditions and resonance position
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The strong sensitivity of the resonance wavelength to 𝑃 indicates the periodic geometry’s role in controlling the optical phase condition and the resonance position. Consequently, variation in the period primarily shifts the spectral location of the dominant emission mode.

mechanism_principle.content: Changing geometry and ITO layer alters spectral position and damping, affecting linewidth and emission concentration
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Changes in these parameters modify both the spectral position and damping of the supported resonance, thereby affecting the linewidth and the fraction of emission concentrated around the principal peak.

mechanism_principle.content: Combined field confinement in the geometry and intrinsic ITO loss enhance absorption, yielding high emittance by Kirchhoff's law
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Consequently, the combination of geometry-induced field confinement and intrinsic optical loss in ITO produces enhanced resonant absorption, which, according to Kirchhoff’s law, gives rise to the observed high thermal emittance.

mechanism_principle.content: TM and TE differences may come from the asymmetrical 1D grating geometry
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The asymmetrical 1D grating geometry of the structure may contribute to the difference between the spectral response at TM and TE polarization.

mechanism_principle.content: k can decrease even as Im(epsilon) rises because k depends on both real and imaginary permittivity
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Although Im(𝜀) increases with temperature, this behavior is physically consistent because 𝑘 depends on both the real and imaginary parts of the complex permittivity. The simultaneous reduction in the magnitude of the negative Re(𝜀) can therefore produce a moderate decrease in 𝑘.

mechanism_principle.content: These spectral changes come from temperature-driven changes in n and k caused by increasing Drude damping
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: These changes originate from the increasing Drude damping, for which Fig. 9 shows a less negative Re(𝜀) together with an increase in Im(𝜀) at elevated temperatures.

mechanism_principle.content: Power absorption rises because thermal photon flux depends strongly on temperature
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: due to the strong temperature dependence of the thermal photon flux.

mechanism_principle.content: QFLS initially rises from stronger photogeneration, then falls because heating increases carrier losses
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting the increasing photogenerated carrier population under stronger above-bandgap illumination... where cell heating increasingly enhances carrier losses.

mechanism_principle.content: Jsc rises because above-bandgap photon flux and photocarrier generation increase
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: because the increasing above-bandgap photon flux produces a progressively larger photocarrier-generation rate.

mechanism_principle.content: Voc first increases with stronger illumination and QFLS, then decreases as higher cell temperature raises recombination and lowers quasi-Fermi-level separation
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The 𝑉oc initially increases as the enhanced illumination raises the photogenerated carrier population and quasi-Fermi-level splitting... subsequently decreases as the increasing 𝑇cell enhances carrier recombination and reduces the achievable quasi-Fermi-level separation.

mechanism_principle.content: FF declines at high temperature because heating and recombination degrade the J-V curve shape
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: where stronger cell heating and recombination progressively degrade the shape of the 𝐽–𝑉 characteristic.

mechanism_principle.content: Jsc stays similar because the radiative spectrum and photogeneration are essentially unchanged
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: because the incident radiative spectrum and the resulting photogeneration are essentially unchanged.

mechanism_principle.content: This measurement is crucial because ITO free-carrier optics are sensitive to thermal processing, crystallinity, and oxygen partial pressure
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Because the free-carrier optical response of ITO is sensitive to thermal processing, crystallinity, and oxygen partial pressure, this step is especially crucial for the current emitter

problem_motivation.content: TPV/PV performance is fundamentally limited by semiconductor bandgaps: sub-bandgap photons are not absorbed, while above-bandgap photons cause thermalization losses, motivating narrowband emitter design matched to the PV cell absorption range.
evidence_spans: However, the photon absorption of a solar cell is constrained by the bandgap of its semiconductor material [4]. Additionally, the absorption of photons with energies well above the bandgap degrades PV cell performance due to thermalization.

problem_motivation.content: Designing an effective narrowband TPV emitter is difficult because multiple competing spectral objectives must be satisfied at once: strong peak emission, peak wavelength within the PV absorption range, minimal FWHM with emission just above the PV cut-off, and very low out-of-band emission.
evidence_spans: However, the most challenging task in achieving a narrowband response is to simultaneously optimize several competing parameters: a strong emission peak, a wavelength of peak emission to be inside the absorption range of the PV cell, a minimal FWHM with an emission range slightly above the PV cell’s absorption cut-off, and very low out-of-band emission.

problem_motivation.content: Promising narrowband emitter designs occupy only a small, structured portion of the overall parameter space, while many regions underperform, so an efficient optimization strategy is needed to identify good geometries and parameters.
evidence_spans: this dataset visualization indicates that the design landscape features both structured, high-performance areas and numerous underperforming regions, highlighting the need for an efficient optimization strategy to systematically identify promising emitter geometries.

these statistics indicate that the dataset contains promising narrowband candidates, but they occupy only a limited portion of the overall parameter space, suggesting that an efficient optimization method is required to effectively find the optimized design parameters for the required performance.

problem_motivation.content: Because the TPV cell performance depends on the emitter spectrum and the emitter’s optical properties vary with temperature, the temperature-dependent optical constants of ITO must be established; this is further motivated by the fact that no prior single study reported both broad-wavelength optical constants and suitable operating-temperature dependence for ITO.
evidence_spans: The TPV cell’s electrical performance strongly depends on the emitter’s emission spectrum, which changes with temperature because the emitter material’s optical characteristics are temperature-dependent. For this reason, before proceeding with the electrothermal analysis, the complex refractive index of the ITO material at different temperatures was evaluated
Since no single published work provided both the necessary broad-wavelength optical constants and an appropriate analysis of their operating-temperature dependence

prior_approach.content: Earlier proposed solutions to the underlying TPV efficiency issue included incorporating back-surface reflectors, altering cell geometry, and using multijunction rather than single-junction cells.
evidence_spans: Previous research recommended numerous solutions to address this issue. Few studies have focused on incorporating a back-surface reflector, altering cell geometry, or developing a multi-junction cell rather than a single-junction cell [5–13].

prior_approach.content: A major prior approach for selective thermal emission is the use of photonic-crystal selective emitters, whose multilayer periodic structures exploit resonances such as Fabry–Pérot and guided-mode resonances, as well as epsilon-near-zero effects.
evidence_spans: In contrast to homogeneous materials, photonic crystal-based selective emitters are found to be a powerful route to achieving selective emission since these multilayer-periodic structures can support different types of resonance modes like Fabry–Pérot (FP) cavity and guided mode resonance and can support epsilon-near-zero effects [18–20].

prior_approach.content: Prior photonic-crystal emitter work commonly used high-temperature refractory-material/dielectric stacks, including Mo, Ta, W, Pt, Si, and Ir based structures with various dielectrics.
evidence_spans: Till now, various high-temperature stable refractory materials, such as molybdenum (Mo), tantalum (Ta), tungsten (W), platinum (Pt), silicon (Si), and iridium (Ir), based structures with various dielectric materials, have been used in photonic crystal-based emitters [21, 22].

prior_approach.content: More recent prior work proposed all-oxide multilayer emitters, including CeO2/MgO and YSZ/MgO composite structures.
evidence_spans: Recently, Song et al proposed all-oxide emitters based on CeO2/MgO and YSZ/MgO composite multilayer structures [25].

prior_approach.content: A common prior design methodology for such photonic structures is forward modeling with parameter sweeps, tuning specified geometric parameters until the desired spectral response is obtained.
evidence_spans: A general strategy for designing such photonic structures is forward modeling, in which the geometric parameters of a specified structure are tuned until the desired spectral response is achieved.

prior_approach.content: ITO–Al2O3 architectures had already been experimentally demonstrated as wavelength-selective thermal emitters, and prior fabrication studies also established patterning routes for such materials, including ITO diffraction gratings made by thermal nanoimprint lithography with RF sputtering, scalable colloidal lithography for patterned ITO emitters, anisotropic dry etching of Al2O3 using BCl3/Cl2/Ar plasmas, and controlled dry etching of ITO-containing multilayers using H2/HCl high-density plasma.
evidence_spans: Indeed, ITO–Al2O3 architectures have previously been experimentally demonstrated for wavelength-selective thermal emission [28].
Hasuike et al. used thermal nanoimprint lithography in conjunction with RF sputtering to experimentally demonstrate an ITO diffraction-grating structure [41]
Dao et al. demonstrated scalable colloidal lithography for patterned ITO-based selective thermal emitters [28].
Anisotropic dry etching of Al2O3 thin films has been experimentally demonstrated using such plasma chemistries [43].

Yoon et al. provided an experimental foundation for anisotropic pattern transfer in ITO by demonstrating controlled dry etching of ITO-containing multilayer structures using H2/HCl-based high-density plasma [44].

prior_approach.content: Prior high-temperature studies indicated that ITO thin films can remain functional at elevated temperatures, though behavior depends on crystallinity, oxygen partial pressure, deposition conditions, and substrate; specifically, Gregory et al. found ITO on alumina remained structurally and chemically stable after 1400 °C exposure, Kim et al. showed temperature-driven optical-property changes were systematic and reversible under controlled oxygen pressure, and Li et al. reported stable conductivity and microstructure during prolonged 1000 °C operation.
evidence_spans: Furthermore, high-temperature studies have demonstrated that ITO thin films can retain useful optical and electrical functionality at elevated temperatures, although their properties depend on crystallinity, oxygen partial pressure, deposition conditions, and the underlying substrate [29–31].
Gregory et al. reported that ITO films deposited on alumina remained structurally and chemically stable even after exposure to 1400 ◦C (1673 K)

More recently, Kim et al. demonstrated that although the optical properties of ITO evolve with temperature because of electron–phonon interactions and oxygen-vacancy redistribution, these changes are systematic and reversible under controlled oxygen partial pressure, indicating that ITO retains its functional optical characteristics at elevated temperatures [30].

In addition, Li et al. reported stable electrical conductivity and microstructural stability of ITO films during prolonged operation at 1000 ◦C, confirming their suitability for harsh thermal environments [31].

prior_limitation.content: Prior TPV/PV approaches suffer practical drawbacks including manufacturability and cost challenges, parasitic absorption, elevated surface-recombination/passivation burdens, and sensitivity to spectral variations/current matching.
evidence_spans: Despite their performance potential, back-surface reflectors can suffer from parasitic absorption in reflector stacks and elevated surface recombination, requiring stringent passivation, while multijunction solar cells remain limited by complex fabrication, extremely high manufacturing costs, and series-connected current-matching sensitivity to spectral variations; on the other hand, complex geometries often increase surface-area-driven recombination and impose difficult passivation and fabrication requirements, which negatively impact practical manufacturability [14–17].

prior_limitation.content: Refractory-material emitters are prone to oxidation at high temperatures, degrading optical performance and thermal stability.
evidence_spans: Although refractory materials exhibit high thermal stability, they are prone to oxidation at high temperatures, which can severely degrade the structure’s optical performance and thermal stability [23].

rejected_alternative.content: Using wide-bandgap oxides such as Al2O3 as the principal absorptive medium is rejected; instead, the design uses ITO as the absorber, while Al2O3 mainly serves dielectric confinement, phase control, and impedance matching.
evidence_spans: In contrast, wide-bandgap dielectric oxides such as Al2O3 generally exhibit comparatively low optical loss in the near-infrared and therefore primarily provide dielectric confinement, phase control, and impedance matching rather than acting as the principal absorptive medium.

rejected_alternative.content: Pursuing the highest conversion efficiency alone is not the main objective; instead, the work prioritizes an all-oxide, oxidation-resistant emitter platform combined with inverse design, direct FDTD verification, temperature-dependent ITO optical modeling, angular-response analysis, and cell-level electrothermal simulation in a unified framework.
evidence_spans: Although the proposed configuration does not provide the highest conversion efficiency among the systems listed in Table 1, its distinguishing feature is the integration of an all-oxide, oxidation-resistant emitter architecture with surrogate-assisted Bayesian inverse design, direct FDTD verification, temperature-dependent ITO optical modeling, angular-response analysis, and cell-level electrothermal simulation within a unified computational framework.

causal_claim.content: Challenges of forward modeling motivate inverse design, where the design task is reframed as optimizing structural parameters to satisfy a target spectral requirement.
evidence_spans: These challenges lead to the inverse-design method, in which the design task is framed as an optimization problem: given a specified spectral requirement, identify the structural parameters that most effectively satisfy it.

causal_claim.content: Machine learning surrogate models accelerate inverse design by replacing repeated costly simulations, enabling much faster assessment of candidate designs and effective exploration of continuous parameter spaces than full-wave simulation.
evidence_spans: Recent progress in machine learning (ML) and surrogate modeling has expedited inverse design by substituting costly repeated simulations with data-driven models that estimate the relationship between design parameters and performance metrics.

After being trained on a sufficiently extensive simulation database, a surrogate model can assess potential designs significantly more quickly than full-wave simulation, enabling effective exploration of continuous parameter spaces.

causal_claim.content: Bayesian optimization improves inverse design by probabilistically selecting new candidates to balance exploitation of promising regions with exploration of uncertain ones.

hypothesis_statement.content: This work hypothesizes that a machine-learning/surrogate-assisted Bayesian inverse design framework, combined with physically relevant spectral constraints, temperature-dependent material modeling, and cell-level electrothermal analysis, can effectively develop oxidation-resistant, spectrally selective all-oxide TPV emitters that meet required performance metrics, including peak emissivity above 0.9.

In this work, we proposed a machine-learning-based inverse design approach to determine the optimal design of all-oxide emitter, which consists of ITO Al2O3 composite structures to achieve peak emissions exceeding 0.9.

By unifying surrogate-assisted inverse design, temperature-resolved ITO dispersion, and cell-level electrothermal analysis, this work establishes a comprehensive computational framework for developing oxidation-resistant, spectrally selective all-oxide emitters for high-temperature TPV energy conversion.

Overall, the obtained results demonstrate that surrogate-assisted Bayesian inverse de-sign of Al2O3/ITO/sapphire architecture with temperature-dependent material modeling and electrothermal analysis can provide an effective computational route for developing spectrally selective TPV emitters in an oxidation-resistant material platform for high-temperature operation.
